title: Hospitality
hookLine: open the door and the table
tomorrow: why did Jesus take three friends along to pray, then find them asleep?

lines: A GUEST LIST IS A MAP.
cards: A guest list is a kind of map: who's close, who owes you, who you'd like to impress.
Jesus is at a dinner in the house of a leading Pharisee, watching guests angle for the best seats, when he turns to the host and redraws the map.

In the Douay-Rheims Bible: "when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, and the blind." Not your friends, he says, not your kin, not rich neighbors who'll invite you back. So who belongs at your table?

teach.b: Catholics have read this in two ways, and both have a real case. The first reads it straight: open the door to people who can't pay you back, and mean the words literally.
Dorothy Day and the Catholic Worker opened houses of hospitality in that spirit, where strangers could eat and sleep. The Rule of Saint Benedict asks monks to receive every guest as Christ himself.

On this reading, a table kept for friends misses the point. The second reading looks at the reason Jesus gives: lest they invite you again, and you're repaid. On this view the trouble isn't friends at the table.
It's a table run like a trade.

Jesus eats with friends himself, with Martha, Mary and Lazarus in Bethany. A family dinner can be holy; what changes it is the chair kept open and a host who isn't keeping score. Here is each one at its best.
The first says: without a real stranger, an open table turns into a warm feeling that costs nothing.
The second says: if every meal has to hold the poor, ordinary family tables start to look like failures, and Jesus never treated them that way.
Both end on the same promise Luke gives: you'll be blessed, because they have nothing to repay you with.

how: Catholics practice hospitality at family tables, in parish meals, and in houses of hospitality like those of the Catholic Worker; Benedictine monasteries receive guests as Christ.

o: the duty to feed your relatives on holidays
a polished dinner party that impresses the guests
an open door and table for a guest, no score kept

p: a table run like a trade
what the second reading warns against

s: Jesus said this at a dinner in a leading Pharisee's house
Luke sets it at a meal, with guests choosing their seats.
Luke says the guests at that dinner chose the lowest seats
Jesus watched them pick the places of honor.
the Rule of Saint Benedict asks that guests be received as Christ
that's how the rule asks monks to welcome every guest.

games.q: you read Luke 14 straight: real strangers at the table. a friend argues family dinners count too. what's her best case?
o: Jesus's warning is about keeping score, and he ate with friends in Bethany.
Luke 14 was only meant for the one Pharisee who hosted Jesus.
the poor are better served by donations than by dinners.
games.why: the reason Jesus gives is repayment, and he shared friends' tables too. the straight reading's best case: without a real stranger, an open table costs nothing.

practice: Open a blank message and write a real invitation: one person, one meal, a day and a time. It might be someone who's been alone lately, or someone who could never return the favor. Send it now, or keep it as a version for tonight.
If you pray, you can pray for whoever ends up in that chair.

wordCard.voice: Hospitality. An open door and an open table, set for a guest by a host who isn't keeping score. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: hospitality. the word Paul uses when he tells the Romans to pursue hospitality (Romans 12:13).

carryVoice: Pocket this one: open table, with a chair for someone who can't pay you back. Rest well.
